Study_Title: ACFix: Guiding LLMs With Mined Common RBAC Practices for Context-Aware Repair of Access Control Vulnerabilities in Smart Contracts
M1_Justification: Combines GPT-4 with static analysis, AST-based code slicing, a mined RBAC taxonomy (49 role-permission pairs from 344,251 contracts), and an iterative generator-validator loop (Sections III–IV).
M2_Justification: Enforces multi-stage validation covering patch syntax/grammar, Solidity compilation, def-use integrity, and semantic access-control enforcement (Sections IV, VII).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on 118 real-world Solidity access-control flaws (94.92% fix rate vs. 52.54% base GPT-4) with baseline comparisons, ablations, and human evaluation (Section VII).
M4_Justification: Commits to source/dataset release and considers human-in-the-loop review, though restricted to Solidity access-control flaws without live production workflow deployment (Sections I, VII).
Key_Strengths: High repair success (94.92%) on 118 real-world Solidity access-control vulnerabilities; empirically mined RBAC taxonomy; multi-layer syntax, compilation, and semantic verification.
Limitations: Risk of overly restrictive access-control patches blocking valid callers; bounded by mined RBAC pairs; limited to Solidity access-control flaws.
Missing_Evidence: DOI, publication year, and formal conference/journal venue in metadata header.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections I, III, IV, VII (Pages 1–13)

Study_Title: PatUntrack: Automated Generating Patch Examples for Issue Reports without Tracked Insecure Code
M1_Justification: Implements VulCoK auto-prompting with BFS Vulnerability-Triggering Path extraction, external golden vulnerability knowledge retrieval, and iterative prompt refinement (Section 3, Fig. 5), without AST patching, compiler checks, or CI/CD integration.
M2_Justification: Assesses generated patch examples strictly via static statement-matching metrics (MatchLine, MatchTrig, MatchFix, Trig@K, Fix@K) and developer usefulness ratings (27/37 replies), with zero compilation, unit testing, or exploit execution (Sections 4.3, 9).
M3_Justification: Evaluated across 5,465 real-world vulnerable issue reports (3,473 test IRs including 2,976 lacking tracked code) plus 76 newly disclosed IRs against six baselines (CodeBERT, Codeium, InCoder, CodeT5, Codex, ChatGPT) with kappa > 0.9 (Sections 4.1–4.3, 9).
M4_Justification: Supports early developer triage on untracked issue reports with practitioner validation on 76 live issues (Section 9), but produces non-verified illustrative examples and provides no public artifact URL.
Key_Strengths: Large-scale 5,465-issue real-world evaluation; retrieval-backed hallucination reduction (VulCoK); practitioner evaluation on 76 newly disclosed issues.
Limitations: Produces illustrative patch examples rather than compilable repository patches; relies exclusively on static lexical/statement matching without build or security testing.
Missing_Evidence: Compilation/execution test validation; public source code or dataset repository URL; formal venue/year metadata.

Study_Title: Securing LLM-Generated Embedded Firmware Through AI Agent-Driven Validation and Patching
M1_Justification: Orchestrates specialized Threat Detection, Performance Optimization, and Compliance agents with AFL++/Syzkaller fuzzers, Clang Static Analyzer, Cppcheck, and QEMU+FreeRTOS runtime instrumentation in an iterative loop (Sections III.D–G).
M2_Justification: Verifies repairs via deterministic unit tests, static analyzer re-scans, coverage-guided fuzzing (AFL++/Syzkaller), and real-time RTOS timing checks (8.6 ms WCET, 195 us jitter) across CWE-120, CWE-362, and CWE-400 (Sections III.F, V).
M3_Justification: Reports 92.4% remediation rate and 95.8% threat-model compliance inside a virtualized QEMU+FreeRTOS environment (Abstract, Section V), but lacks real-world firmware CVE benchmarks and external AVR tool comparisons.
M4_Justification: Addresses explicit CWEs (CWE-120, CWE-362, CWE-400) and real-time embedded constraints, but is tested only in virtualized QEMU emulation without physical hardware validation or released artifacts (Section VI).
Key_Strengths: Comprehensive static, dynamic fuzzing (AFL++/Syzkaller), and real-time WCET/jitter validation in virtualized FreeRTOS; multi-agent architecture.
Limitations: Evaluated only on LLM-generated firmware in QEMU emulation rather than physical microcontrollers or real-world CVEs; relies primarily on GPT-4; artifact release deferred to future work.
Missing_Evidence: Real-world embedded CVE benchmark results; public code/dataset repository URL; bibliographic venue/year.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections I, III.D–G, V, VI (Pages 1–9)

Study_Title: SecureFixAgent: A Hybrid LLM Agent for Automated Python Static Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Couples Bandit SAST scanning with locally hosted LoRA fine-tuned LLMs (<=8B: DeepSeek Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder, CodeLlama, CodeGemma) in an automated detect–repair–validate feedback loop generating patches and explanations (Sections III.A–D, Fig. 1).
M2_Justification: Re-scans patched files iteratively with Bandit until convergence (typically <=3 rounds) and assesses explanation quality via a 15-user study (Sections III.B, V), but performs no unit test execution or dynamic exploit verification.
M3_Justification: Benchmarks 6 open-weight models (base vs. LoRA fine-tuned) against Bandit-only and LLM-only baselines across synthetic and real-world Python CVEs, measuring fix accuracy (up to 87.83%), false-positive reduction (to 8.11%), and Likert scores (4.5/5) (Sections IV–V, Fig. 3, Table IV).
M4_Justification: Enables privacy-preserving local execution on <=8B models with developer-oriented explanations (n = 15), yet remains limited to Python Bandit rules without CI/CD PR automation or public code links.
Key_Strengths: Automated local SAST (Bandit) + LoRA fine-tuned <=8B LLM loop; quantitative false-positive and fix-accuracy analysis across 6 models; 15-participant explanation study.
Limitations: Limited to Python and Bandit-detectable rules; lacks functional regression test execution or dynamic exploit checks; difficulty with multi-file repairs.
Missing_Evidence: Functional unit-test pass rates; public source code/dataset repository URL; publication year/venue metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections III.A–D, V, VI.B; Fig. 1, Fig. 3; Table IV (Pages 1–6)

Study_Title: LLMSecConfig: An LLM-Based Approach for Fixing Software Container Misconfigurations
M1_Justification: Integrates Checkov static scanning, RAG retrieval, YAML syntax validation, and a dual-loop (inner syntax retry + outer security retry) repair pipeline with structured logging for Kubernetes manifests (Sections III, IV, V.A).
M2_Justification: Validates YAML syntax (Parse Success Rate) and Checkov security policy compliance (Pass Rate, Security Improvement, Introduced Errors) iteratively (Sections IV, V.A), but lacks live Kubernetes cluster deployment or runtime functional testing.
M3_Justification: Evaluates 1,000 real-world Kubernetes manifests mined from ArtifactHub across multiple LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, mistral-large-2407), reporting Parse Success Rate, Pass Rate (up to 94%), Pass Steps, AUC, and newly introduced errors (Sections IV.B, V).
M4_Justification: Publicly shares code and data on Figshare (https://figshare.com/s/2a9be8ccfbec9d8ba199), targets production ArtifactHub Kubernetes manifests, and tracks regression misconfigurations (Sections IV.A–B, IX).
Key_Strengths: Large-scale evaluation on 1,000 real-world Kubernetes manifests; dual syntactic and Checkov security retry loops; explicit regression error tracking; public Figshare artifacts.
Limitations: Scoped to Kubernetes YAML configurations and static Checkov policies without live cluster runtime verification.
Missing_Evidence: Live Kubernetes cluster functional/admission testing; formal DOI and publication venue metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections III, IV.A–B, V.A, VIII, IX (Pages 1–13)

Study_Title: A New Era in Software Security: Towards Self-Healing Software via Large Language Models and Formal Verification
M1_Justification: Couples the ESBMC Bounded Model Checker (abstract interpretation, constraint programming, SMT symbolic model checking) with an LLM in a counterexample-guided detect–repair–reverify loop enforcing a 10-second verification budget (Section V, Fig. 1).
M2_Justification: Applies formal SMT-based bounded model checking (ESBMC) to both extract exact line/variable counterexamples and formally re-verify elimination of buffer overflow, integer overflow, null dereference, and division-by-zero flaws (Sections IV–VI, Fig. 2).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on 50,000 C programs from FormAI across five major vulnerability classes, comparing single-step and multi-iteration ESBMC-AI repairs against standalone LLMs (>90% on buffer/array bounds, >80% on null-dereference/div-by-zero) (Abstract, Sections VI–VII).
M4_Justification: Published as an installable PyPI package (ESBMC-AI 0.5.1), offers interactive chat and automated fix modes, targets explicit C CWEs, and enforces a 10-second verification bound compatible with IDE/CI pipelines (Sections V.A–B, VII).
Key_Strengths: Mathematically sound SMT bounded model checking for counterexample guidance and post-patch verification; massive 50,000-program evaluation; installable PyPI release (ESBMC-AI 0.5.1).
Limitations: Evaluated on single-file FormAI C programs; bounded model checking faces limits on complex external headers and multi-file projects.
Missing_Evidence: Multi-file real-world CVE repository benchmarks; formal DOI and venue metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections IV, V.A–B, VI, VII; Fig. 1, Fig. 2 (Pages 1–10)

Study_Title: CFCEval: Evaluating Security Aspects in Code Generated by Large Language Models
M1_Justification: Defines an offline evaluation framework (CFCEval) and similarity metric (ELRM) for scoring LLM code outputs, without integrating SAST/DAST analyzers, AST patch generators, or CI/CD repair loops (Sections II–IV).
M2_Justification: Uses reference-based structural/lexical similarity (ELRM), LLM-as-judge (GPT-Tagger/GPT-Scorer), human adjudication, and spot-check tests/static scans (Sections II.B–C, V), lacking full-scale execution-based exploit/regression validation.
M3_Justification: Constructs MLVBench to mitigate data contamination and runs a pilot evaluation of code LLMs across four quality dimensions, comparing ELRM against BLEU and CodeBLEU (Abstract, Sections III–IV, VII).
M4_Justification: Provides the MLVBench benchmark and automated scoring protocol (with GitHub appendix referenced), but serves as an offline evaluation framework rather than an operational repair tool (Sections II, VII).
Key_Strengths: Mitigates train-test leakage via MLVBench; introduces fine-grained Element-Level Relevance Metric (ELRM) calibrated against human judgments.
Limitations: Pilot-scale evaluation framework rather than an end-to-end automated repair pipeline; relies primarily on reference similarity and LLM-as-judge with only spot-check test/static verification.
Missing_Evidence: Full-scale multi-language execution-based validation; standalone repair tool deployment; DOI/year/venue metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections II.B–C, III, IV, V, VII; Figs. 4–5 (Pages 1–10)

Study_Title: Enhanced automated code vulnerability repair using large language models
M1_Justification: Formulates a structured line-level diff representation (line_bef, line_af, <MID>, <sep>) with QLoRA fine-tuning and AWQ/GPTQ quantization for Code Llama and Mistral (Pages 1, 10, 17), operating as a standalone model without SAST/DAST or CI/CD integration.
M2_Justification: Measures patch quality solely via static exact-match ('Perfect Predictions') against reference commits on dataset splits, with zero compilation checks, unit testing, SAST re-scans, or exploit execution (Pages 1, 17).
M3_Justification: Evaluates fine-tuned Code Llama and Mistral on C/C++ datasets (Big-Vul/CVEFixes), constructing a deduplicated leak-free test split that exposes a 57% to 26% drop from contaminated splits and benchmarking against VulRepair across decoding settings (Pages 1, 16–17).
M4_Justification: Reduces inference VRAM to 5.5 GB via AWQ quantization and supports CWE-conditioned multi-location C/C++ diffs (Pages 10, 17), but remains an unverified offline model without public deployment tooling.
Key_Strengths: Rigorous dataset decontamination exposing train-test leakage inflation (57% vs. 26%); compact structured diff format; low-VRAM (5.5 GB) quantization analysis.
Limitations: Evaluated exclusively via static exact-match ('Perfect Prediction') without compilation, functional tests, or security validation; constrained to small beam sizes (<=5) and C/C++ functions.
Missing_Evidence: Compilation, unit-test, or SAST/DAST validation of generated patches; public source code repository URL.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Methodology, Results & Discussion (Pages 1, 10, 16–17; Fig. 3; Table 4)

Study_Title: Benchmarking Automated Security Patch Backporting: How Far Are We?
M1_Justification: Applies tree-sitter AST parsing for hierarchical commit-to-file-to-function patch alignment and benchmarks five backporting systems including program analysis, PortGPT, and executable-feedback LLM agents (Sections 3.2, 3.4, Table 11), functioning primarily as a benchmark framework.
M2_Justification: Pairs a five-level hierarchical static matcher (L1 Exact Match through L2–L5 structural completeness with manual review) with dynamic executable validation on 45 cases using project test suites and PoC exploits (Abstract, Section 3.3, Fig. 3, Table 11).
M3_Justification: Evaluates five tools across 1,234 real-world C/C++ security backporting cases (cross-version, cross-branch, cross-repository) plus 45 dynamically tested PoC cases, stratified into Type-I to Type-IV complexity with failure root-cause analysis and kappa = 0.972–1.000 (Abstract, Sections 3.2–3.4, Fig. 3, Table 11).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the 1,234-case Porting Benchmark dataset, framework, and scripts on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21785770), targeting real-world C/C++ repository maintenance workflows (Abstract, Data Availability Statement).
Key_Strengths: Large-scale 1,234-case real-world security backporting benchmark; dual static (L1–L5) and dynamic PoC + test-suite validation; high inter-rater reliability (kappa >= 0.972); public Zenodo release.
Limitations: Targets security patch backporting (adapting existing fixes) rather than novel vulnerability repair; dynamic PoC validation covers a 45-case subset; C/C++ only.
Missing_Evidence: Dynamic PoC execution across the full 1,234-case corpus; evaluation on non-C/C++ ecosystems.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections 3.2–3.4, 6–7; Fig. 3; Table 11; Data Availability (Pages 1, 6, 11)

Study_Title: A Multi-Dataset Evaluation of Models for Automated Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Fine-tunes standalone CodeBERT and CodeT5 models on tokenized source-code pairs without SAST/DAST tools, AST-guided patch generation, iterative feedback loops, or CI/CD integration (Sections 3–4).
M2_Justification: Assesses generated patches solely via static code-similarity metrics (CodeBLEU and CrystalBLEU) without compilation, unit test suites, static analyzer re-scans, or exploit testing, noting this as a construct validity threat (Sections 4, 7; Table 2).
M3_Justification: Benchmarks CodeBERT and CodeT5 across six datasets covering four languages (Go, PHP, MegaVul_C_2023, MegaVul_C_2024, Vul4J, CodeParrot), analyzing both in-distribution and out-of-distribution cross-dataset generalization and run-to-run variance (Sections 4–6; Table 2).
M4_Justification: Publicly shares code and datasets on Zenodo across four programming languages (C, Java, Go, PHP) (Sections 4.1, 9), yet remains an offline fine-tuning study lacking execution verification or workflow integration.
Key_Strengths: Multi-dataset, four-language evaluation (C, Java, Go, PHP) quantifying in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution generalization; public Zenodo release.
Limitations: Relies exclusively on CodeBLEU/CrystalBLEU similarity metrics without compilation, functional tests, or exploit checks; sharp accuracy degradation out-of-distribution.
Missing_Evidence: Compilation, unit-test, or security validation of generated patches; formal peer-reviewed venue metadata.

Study_Title: CVE-Bench: Benchmarking LLM-based Software Engineering Agent's Ability to Repair Real-World CVE Vulnerabilities
M1_Justification: Constructs an interactive containerized agent harness allowing SWE-agent to execute shell navigation and static analysis commands during multi-step CVE patching (Abstract, Section 2), functioning as a benchmark harness rather than a new production repair tool.
M2_Justification: Verifies candidate patches via executable project unit test suites inside simulated containers and classifies failure modes (locate fail, loop out, unit test fail) (Section 3, Fig. 3), but lacks dedicated PoC exploit replay or post-patch DAST/sanitizer checks.
M3_Justification: Benchmarks SWE-agent across 509 real-world CVEs from 120 open-source repositories spanning four programming languages under black-box, intermediate, and white-box settings across GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and Llama-3 (Abstract, Sections 3, 6).
M4_Justification: Covers 509 real-world open-source CVEs across four languages in reproducible containers, though agent fix rate peaks at 21% and tested agents/models remain narrow (Abstract, Section 6).
Key_Strengths: 509 real-world CVEs across 120 repositories and four languages; black-box vs. white-box observability analysis; detailed failure taxonomy.
Limitations: Tests only SWE-agent across three LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-3); max repair success is 21%; relies on unit tests without dedicated PoC exploit verification.
Missing_Evidence: Explicit public repository URL in text; dedicated exploit/sanitizer post-patch checks.

Study_Title: Well Begun is Half Done: Location-Aware and Trace-Guided Iterative Automated Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Integrates vulnerability localization, hunk prediction, CoT LLM patch synthesis, CrashRepair fuzzing/taint trace analysis, and iterative candidate selection in the closed-loop LoopRepair pipeline (Sections 3.1–3.3).
M2_Justification: Compiles patches, runs Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) exploit tests, synthesizes additional fuzzed PoVs via CrashRepair to prevent overfitting, screens for newly introduced CWEs, and performs manual correctness verification (Abstract, Sections 3.3, 8).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on 40 real-world C/C++ vulnerabilities in VulnLoc+ across six vulnerability classes against NMT, program-analysis, and LLM APR baselines, separating plausible (27) from manually verified correct fixes (15) (Abstract, Sections 8–9).
M4_Justification: Open-sources generated patches and addresses real-world C/C++ vulnerabilities across six CWE types, though evaluated on 40 vulnerabilities with manual inspection by three volunteers (Sections 8–9).
Key_Strengths: PoV exploit execution + CrashRepair fuzzing against test overfitting; taint-trace patch ranking; checks for newly introduced vulnerabilities; separates plausible (27) vs. correct (15) fixes.
Limitations: Evaluated on 40 C/C++ vulnerabilities; fails if upstream localization misses; relies on volunteer manual correctness review.
Missing_Evidence: Public source code repository URL in text; production CI/CD deployment.

Study_Title: CWEFT: CWE-Aware Evaluation of Free-Text vs. Typed Prompts
M1_Justification: Implements a Dockerized Vul4J CLI harness applying whole-file patches from three frontier LLMs across four controlled prompt conditions with automated logging and retries (Section 3, Pages 6–7), lacking SAST/DAST feedback loops or IDE/PR integration.
M2_Justification: Evaluates every patch on a four-tier PoV-aware hierarchy (L0 compile failure, L1 compiles/PoV fails, L2 PoV passes/regression fails, L3 PoV and full regression suite pass) in isolated Docker containers with exact McNemar testing (Abstract, Pages 6–7).
M3_Justification: Assesses 504 generated patches across 42 real-world Java vulnerabilities in Vul4J spanning 15 CWEs using Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Pro across four controlled ablation conditions with significance testing (p = 0.049) (Abstract, Section 7).
M4_Justification: Releases the full replication package and data on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21672348) with deterministic Docker execution, though limited to single-shot whole-file Java repair with 19.8% best fix rate and no manual security audit (Pages 7, 13).
Key_Strengths: Rigorous L0–L3 separation of compilation, PoV exploit closure, and functional regression; controlled ablation across Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Pro; public Zenodo replication package.
Limitations: Single-shot whole-file prompting without iterative feedback; low overall fix rate (19.8% best, 3.1% on improper input validation); omits manual security review.
Missing_Evidence: Formal conference/journal venue name in header metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Experimental Setup & Construct Validity; Section 7; Data Availability (Pages 1, 6–7, 13)

Study_Title: PortGPT: Towards Automated Backporting Using Large Language Models
M1_Justification: Implements an end-to-end LLM backporting agent combining Git commit-history summarization, file/symbol localization, per-hunk adaptation, automated format/context mismatch recovery, and iterative compiler feedback loops (Abstract, Section 3, Fig. 2).
M2_Justification: Incorporates compiler feedback during generation and relies primarily on manual inspection against ground-truth backports for final validation (Abstract, Section 8), lacking automated PoC exploit execution across the full benchmark.
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on 1,815 existing backporting cases (89.15% success) and 146 newly curated complex cases (62.33% success) across multiple projects and languages against SOTA backporting baselines (Abstract, Section 9).
M4_Justification: Achieved real-world upstream adoption with 9 backported patches accepted and merged into the Linux kernel, alongside multi-branch/multi-language support and automated Git/compiler integration (Abstract, Section 1).
Key_Strengths: Real-world upstream impact (9 patches merged into the Linux kernel); large-scale 1,815 + 146 case evaluation; automated context-mismatch recovery and compiler feedback.
Limitations: Addresses security patch backporting rather than zero-day patch creation; final validation relies heavily on manual inspection rather than automated dynamic exploit replay.
Missing_Evidence: Automated dynamic exploit validation; explicit public repository URL; formal publication year/venue metadata.

Study_Title: SEC-bench: Automated Benchmarking of LLM Agents on Real-World Software Security Tasks
M1_Justification: Constructs SECVERIFIER, a multi-agent scaffold that automatically builds Dockerized repositories, generates build/test harnesses, reproduces vulnerabilities, and evaluates LLM coding agents on PoC synthesis and patching (Abstract, Section 3).
M2_Justification: Enforces three-round patch inspection and automated sanitizer-backed verification requiring that (1) the PoC triggers memory sanitizers at the base commit, (2) the patch applies cleanly, and (3) the PoC no longer triggers sanitizer errors post-patch (Page 5).
M3_Justification: Curates 200 verified real-world vulnerabilities across 29 open-source projects (from 898 candidates at $0.87/instance) and evaluates multiple SOTA LLM coding agents on PoC generation (up to 18.0%) and patching (up to 34.0%) (Abstract, Table 1, Section 5).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases open-source code (GitHub), dataset (HuggingFace), and leaderboard with containerized reproducible environments, though scoped to sanitizer-detectable C/C++ projects (Abstract, Section 5).
Key_Strengths: Deterministic pre/post-patch sanitizer PoC verification; 200 verified real-world vulnerabilities across 29 projects; public GitHub, HuggingFace, and leaderboard releases.
Limitations: Restricted to C/C++ projects triggerable by memory-safety sanitizers; agent patching success peaks at 34.0%.
Missing_Evidence: Non-C/C++ language coverage; formal conference/journal venue and year metadata.

Study_Title: Multi2Fixer: A Coordinator-Proposer Based Multi-Agent Framework for Fixing Multi-Hunk Bugs
M1_Justification: Implements a Coordinator-Proposer multi-agent architecture integrating static hunk-dependency graph construction, repair-order scheduling, cluster-based candidate selection, structural syntax fallback checks, and iterative patch refinement (Abstract, Section 3, Page 6).
M2_Justification: Enforces structural syntax/signature checks and executes benchmark test suites/oracles across five repair rounds per bug (Sections 3, 7), though security benchmarks (VUL4J, SEC-bench, PatchEval) are evaluated alongside general bugs without post-patch regression-CWE scanning.
M3_Justification: Evaluated across 835 Defects4J bugs and three vulnerability benchmarks (VUL4J: 24/79; SEC-bench multi-hunk: 11/65; PatchEval multi-hunk: 19/120) spanning Java, C++, JavaScript, Go, and Python against multiple APR baselines and LLMs (GPT-3.5, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (Abstract, Sections 7–8).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases full code, configurations, and data pipelines on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/21223018), handles multi-file/multi-hunk edits across five languages, and requires no oracle fault localization (Abstract, Section 8, Data Availability).
Key_Strengths: Static hunk-dependency graph scheduling for coordinated multi-file/multi-hunk repair; strong cross-language vulnerability results across VUL4J, SEC-bench, and PatchEval; public Zenodo artifacts.
Limitations: High failure rate (68.75%) on bugs with 10+ unrepaired hunks or complex bidirectional dependencies; framed broadly around multi-hunk APR.
Missing_Evidence: Explicit post-patch security regression scanning for newly introduced CWEs; DOI in metadata header.

Study_Title: HMF: Enhancing reentrancy vulnerability detection and repair with a hybrid model framework
M1_Justification: Pairs a CNN+MLP detector extracting high-attention vulnerable lines with a four-part knowledge-aware LLM repair prompt (vulnerable/fixed pairs, CEI/transfer/send patterns, attention lines) (Sections 3.2–3.3), without SAST/compiler re-scan loops or CI/CD integration.
M2_Justification: Measures repair rate gains (+9.62%) and conducts a developer user study on smart contract repair (Abstract, Section 7), without formal symbolic verification, dynamic EVM fuzzing, or automated functional test-suite execution.
M3_Justification: Evaluates detection (accuracy, recall, precision, F1) and reentrancy repair (+9.62% over baselines) on SmartBugs-derived datasets with component ablation studies and a user study (Abstract, Section 7).
M4_Justification: Scoped solely to Solidity reentrancy flaws and explicitly declares under Data Availability that no datasets were generated or released, with no public code repository or deployment integration (Section 7, Data Availability, Page 25).
Key_Strengths: Couples DL attention-based line localization with domain-specific CEI smart contract repair patterns; includes ablation and user studies.
Limitations: Narrowly scoped to Solidity reentrancy vulnerabilities; no public code or dataset release; lacks formal verification or dynamic exploit execution.
Missing_Evidence: Public code/dataset repository; functional regression or symbolic security verification of repaired contracts.

Study_Title: SPVR: syntax-to-prompt vulnerability repair based on large language models
M1_Justification: Parses syntax trees into Minimal Error Subtrees (METs) and applies static syntax-check rules (bounds, pointer/initialization checks) plus CWE descriptions to build structured prompts and extract repaired AST subtrees (Abstract, Section 3.4, Appendix A), lacking iterative compiler/SAST feedback loops.
M2_Justification: Evaluates generated patches against ground-truth developer fixes (repairing 143/547 C/C++ vulnerabilities with GPT-4) and tests on 300 post-cutoff vulnerabilities (Abstract, Section 5, Page 24), without executing PoC exploits or dynamic sanitizers.
M3_Justification: Benchmarks SPVR across multiple LLMs on 547 real-world C/C++ vulnerabilities from CVEFixes (Top 25 CWEs) plus an out-of-time validation set of 300 recent vulnerabilities to prevent memorization bias (Abstract, Sections 4.1, 5, Page 24).
M4_Justification: Provides a model-agnostic, low-overhead syntax-rule prompt generator covering Top-25 CWEs in C/C++ with post-cutoff testing, though no public repository link or CI/CD integration is established (Section 4.1, Page 24).
Key_Strengths: AST Minimal Error Subtree extraction and static rule-augmented prompting; post-cutoff 300-vulnerability validation mitigating pre-training leakage.
Limitations: Single-pass prompt generation without iterative compiler/SAST/exploit feedback loops; restricted to C/C++ functions.
Missing_Evidence: Dynamic PoC/sanitizer verification; public artifact repository URL; peer-reviewed journal/conference metadata.

Study_Title: SecureMind: A Framework for Benchmarking Large Language Models in Memory Bug Detection and Repair
M1_Justification: Builds a Python benchmarking API that retrieves vulnerable repos, applies source-level code obfuscations, sweeps decoding parameters, and queries LLMs across prompt templates (Sections 3.2, 4.3, Fig. 5), acting as a benchmark harness rather than a tool-integrated repair agent.
M2_Justification: Evaluates repair using developer reference patches and project unit test cases retrieved for the repair subset (Section 4.2, Page 6), without post-patch sanitizer/fuzzer exploit replay or multi-step repair refinement.
M3_Justification: Evaluates 10 LLMs (including 7 reasoning models such as ChatGPT-o1 and DeepSeek R1) across 16K memory-safety samples (8 CWEs, assembly and obfuscated variants) and a 23-sample executable repair subset, analyzing hyperparameter sensitivity and obfuscation robustness (Abstract, Sections 4.2–5, Fig. 5).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases an open-source Python framework and benchmark datasets covering 8 memory-safety CWEs with reproducible cloud execution configurations (Abstract, Section 8).
Key_Strengths: Systematic evaluation of 10 LLMs (7 reasoning models) under source-level obfuscation and decoding sweeps; open-source Python benchmarking API.
Limitations: Executable vulnerability repair evaluation is limited to a small 23-sample subset (max 37% repair rate with ChatGPT-o1); models degrade sharply under obfuscation.
Missing_Evidence: Larger-scale executable repair benchmark beyond 23 samples; explicit GitHub URL in excerpt.

Study_Title: CloudFix: Automated Policy Repair for Cloud Access Control Policies Using Large Language Models
M1_Justification: Integrates Quacky quantitative symbolic policy analysis for fault localization with LLM patch generation and SMT solver formal verification in an automated cloud IAM policy repair pipeline (Abstract, Sections III–V).
M2_Justification: Formally verifies every LLM-generated AWS IAM policy repair against allowed and denied access request specifications via SMT solvers (Quacky), guaranteeing semantic compliance (Abstract, Section VIII).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on 282 real-world faulty AWS IAM policies (444 statements across 92 AWS services, mined from 9,968 AWS re:Post posts) across varying request-suite sizes against baseline methods (Abstract, Section IV.A–B, Table I).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases both the CloudFix tool and the 282-policy dataset on GitHub (https://github.com/bethelhall/fixmypolicy), targets real-world cloud IAM policies, and uses fast SMT verification suited to cloud governance pipelines (Abstract, Sections VIII–IX).
Key_Strengths: End-to-end symbolic localization + LLM synthesis + formal SMT verification for cloud IAM policies; 282 real-world AWS policies; public GitHub tool and dataset release.
Limitations: Scoped to AWS IAM JSON policies; relies on synthetic allowed/denied request specifications rather than live production traffic logs.
Missing_Evidence: Evaluation on multi-cloud policy formats (Azure/GCP/Terraform); formal DOI/year/venue metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections IV.A–B, VII, VIII, IX; Table I (Pages 1, 5–6, 11–12)

Study_Title: Rethinking the Capability of Fine-Tuned Language Models for Automated Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Constructs the Dockerized L-AVRBench execution harness and semantic-preserving program transformation pipeline to evaluate fine-tuned AVR models (VulRepair, VulMaster, VulAdvisor) (Abstract, Sections 6–7), rather than proposing a tool-integrated repair generator.
M2_Justification: Demonstrates the invalidity of static match metrics (EM, BLEU, CodeBLEU) and enforces Dockerized test-based execution validation in L-AVRBench supplemented by manual functional and security correctness auditing (Abstract, Section 7, Data Availability).
M3_Justification: Evaluates fine-tuned AVR models across leakage-controlled chronological splits (exposing >85% commit overlap and EM drops from 18.30% to 4.96% for VulRepair and 20.47% to 5.15% for VulMaster), semantic-preserving perturbations, and 70 executable cases from ExtractFix/Magma/CVEs (Tables 3–4, Section 7).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the implementation, benchmark instances, Docker images, and evaluation scripts on GitHub (https://github.com/rimwoohan/L-AVRBench) for reproducible execution-based AVR benchmarking (Data Availability, Page 12).
Key_Strengths: Exposes >85% train-test commit overlap in standard AVR benchmarks; provides Dockerized test-based L-AVRBench; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Evaluates three fine-tuned models (VulRepair, VulMaster, VulAdvisor) and 70 executable cases due to manual adaptation overhead.
Missing_Evidence: Evaluation on frontier prompt-based/agentic LLMs; DOI metadata.

Study_Title: Diverse LLMs vs. Vulnerabilities: Who Detects and Fixes Them Better?
M1_Justification: Builds DVDR-LLM, an ensemble orchestration framework combining 10 diverse LLMs (Llama3, Gemma2, CodeLlama, Mistral, etc.) across multi-file contexts with consensus voting thresholds (Abstract, Sections 4, 6), lacking SAST/DAST tools or compiler feedback loops.
M2_Justification: Assesses patch verification classification tasks (SVD2/SVD4) and static weighted repair quality metrics across 10 LLMs (Sections 4, 6), performing no automated compilation, unit testing, or dynamic PoC exploit execution.
M3_Justification: Evaluates 10 LLMs and their ensemble across single-function, multi-function, and multi-file Linux kernel vulnerabilities, reporting recall/F1 deltas (+18% recall, +11.8% F1 multi-file) and threshold trade-offs (Abstract, Section 4, Fig. 2).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases source code on GitHub (https://github.com/Erroristotle/DVDR_LLM) and addresses multi-file Linux kernel vulnerabilities, yet remains limited to C/Linux kernel CVEs without automated build/exploit validation (Abstract, Section 5).
Key_Strengths: 10-LLM ensemble evaluation across single-function and multi-file Linux kernel vulnerabilities; public GitHub repository.
Limitations: Lacks static/dynamic analysis feedback loops, compilation, or PoC exploit execution; trade-off between detection recall and verification false positives.
Missing_Evidence: Execution-based or PoC validation of generated patches; formal publication year/venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: Secure coding with AI – from detection to repair
M1_Justification: Pairs static security scanners with zero-shot LLM prompting (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1) and post-patch static re-scanning in a detect-and-repair workflow (Abstract, Section 6.2), without AST-guided repair or CI/CD integration.
M2_Justification: Verifies modified snippets via static scanner re-scanning and manual author security review (Abstract, Page 1), lacking automated functional test suites or dynamic exploit replay.
M3_Justification: Screens 2,315 real-world C, C++, and C# snippets from DevGPT (56 vulnerabilities across 48 files) and conducts longitudinal comparisons across Oct 2024 and Sep 2025 with GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.1 (repairing 42–44/56) (Abstract, Section 6.2).
M4_Justification: Builds on the public DevGPT corpus and shares artifacts on GitHub covering C, C++, and C# with CWE mappings (Abstract, Data Availability, Page 36), though scoped to 48 files without a standalone repair tool.
Key_Strengths: Real-world DevGPT developer-AI interaction dataset (2,315 snippets); longitudinal comparison across GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.1; combined static re-scan and manual audit.
Limitations: Small repaired sample (56 vulnerabilities across 48 files); zero-shot prompting only; lacks functional unit testing or dynamic PoC execution.
Missing_Evidence: Functional regression testing; standalone open-source repair tool implementation.

Study_Title: SYNTHFIX: Adaptive Neuro-Symbolic Code Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Uses static AST/CFG complexity features in a neural Router Model to dynamically route training batches between SFT and compiler-informed symbolic Reward Fine-Tuning across CodeT5, CodeGen, CodeLLaMA-7B, and StarCoder2-7B (Abstract, Section 3, Limitations), without IDE/CI runtime integration.
M2_Justification: Applies compiler-informed symbolic rewards during RFT training, while final evaluation uses static CodeBLEU, CrystalBLEU, and Exact Match metrics without dynamic exploit replay or post-patch security scanning (Abstract, Tables 1–2, Limitations).
M3_Justification: Benchmarks four model families on FixJS (JavaScript) and CodeFlaws (C), comparing SFT-only, RFT-only, fixed hybrid, and adaptive router-scheduled SYNTHFIX with ablation and convergence studies (Tables 1–2, Page 26860).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases MIT-licensed code and data on GitHub (https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/SynthFix) covering C and JavaScript (Abstract, Page 26857), though tested only on academic function benchmarks.
Key_Strengths: Adaptive AST/CFG-guided SFT/RFT training router with compiler symbolic rewards; evaluated across 4 LLMs on C and JavaScript; MIT-licensed GitHub release.
Limitations: Final benchmark evaluation relies on static similarity/exact-match metrics without dynamic exploit validation; untested on large industrial repositories.
Missing_Evidence: Post-patch dynamic execution or PoC security verification; DOI metadata.

Study_Title: ContractTinker: LLM-Empowered Vulnerability Repair for Real-World Smart Contracts
M1_Justification: Combines static program analysis (dependency graph construction and Contextual Dependency Graph slicing) with LLM entity recognition and multi-step Chain-of-Thought repair (attack analysis, mitigation strategy, patch synthesis) (Abstract, Sections 2.2–2.3).
M2_Justification: Evaluates generated patches via manual inspection into valid fixes (48%), minor-modification fixes (21%), logic-modification needed, and irreparable (Abstract, Section 4), lacking automated symbolic verification or dynamic EVM exploit fuzzing.
M3_Justification: Tested on 48 real-world high-risk smart contract vulnerabilities from third-party audit reports (Abstract, Section 4), without quantitative comparisons against prior smart contract repair baselines.
M4_Justification: Demonstrates a functional prototype with a YouTube demo targeting real-world smart contract audits, though struggling with complex business logic (e.g., TWAP price manipulation) and omitting a public code repository URL (Abstract, Section 4).
Key_Strengths: Integrates static dependency slicing (CDG) with multi-step Chain-of-Thought reasoning on 48 real-world high-risk smart contract audit vulnerabilities.
Limitations: Small 48-vulnerability sample; relies on manual inspection without automated symbolic/dynamic verification; struggles with complex business logic; no code repo URL.
Missing_Evidence: Automated formal/dynamic verification; quantitative baseline comparisons; open-source code repository URL.

Study_Title: Bridging Code Property Graphs and Language Models for Program Analysis
Venue: SVM '26 (4th International Workshop on Software Vulnerability Management)
M1_Justification: Implements codebadger, a Dockerized Model Context Protocol (MCP) server integrating Joern's Code Property Graph engine (slicing, taint tracking, data-flow analysis) with GitHub Copilot Agent and Claude Sonnet 4.5 for repository-scale auditing and patching (Abstract, Sections 4–5).
M2_Justification: Demonstrates finding/exploiting a zero-day buffer overflow in libtiff and generating a first-attempt patch for CVE-2025-6021 in libxml2 via qualitative case studies (Abstract, Section 5), lacking quantitative validation across a benchmark suite.
M3_Justification: Evaluation comprises solely three qualitative use cases (GGML auditing, libtiff exploitation, CVE-2025-6021 libxml2 patching) with no quantitative benchmark metrics, baselines, or fix rates, as noted in Section 6 (Abstract, Sections 5–6).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases open-source Dockerized MCP server code on GitHub (https://github.com/lekssays/codebadger), integrates with GitHub Copilot Agent, scales to 246k LOC / 8,000+ methods, and demonstrates real-world zero-day impact (Abstract, Sections 5.1, 6.1, 7).
Key_Strengths: Practical MCP server bridging Joern CPG slicing/taint analysis with agentic IDE workflows; scales to 246k LOC repositories; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Purely qualitative case-study evaluation (1 patched CVE) without benchmark fix rates or baseline comparisons; high Joern RAM footprint on large repos.
Missing_Evidence: Quantitative benchmark evaluation across multiple CVEs and baselines.

Study_Title: How Well Do Large Language Models Serve as End-to-End Secure Code Agents for Python?
M1_Justification: Couples CodeQL and Bandit static analysis tools with LLM prompting (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama, CodeGeeX2) in a feedback-driven self-iterative detection and repair loop (Sections 2.5, 10), lacking AST-guided patching or automated PR generation.
M2_Justification: Verifies generated and repaired Python snippets via CodeQL and Bandit static re-scans plus manual review across ~4,900 code pieces (Abstract, Sections 2.5, 10), without unit test execution or dynamic exploit replay.
M3_Justification: Evaluates four LLMs across 484 SecurityEval tasks and ~4,900 generated/repaired Python snippets across four RQs (secure generation, self-detection, cross-model vs. self-repair achieving 33.2%–59.6% fix rates, and SAST-guided iterative repair) (Abstract, Sections 3.1, 10).
M4_Justification: Shares a public companion repository with results and uses standard open-source SAST tools (CodeQL, Bandit) on consumer hardware, though restricted to synthetic SecurityEval Python prompts without repository integration (Sections 2.5, 3.2, 10).
Key_Strengths: Large-scale empirical evaluation of ~4,900 Python snippets across 4 LLMs comparing self-repair, cross-model repair, and SAST-guided loops.
Limitations: Evaluated on synthetic SecurityEval prompts rather than multi-file repositories; relies on static analysis (CodeQL/Bandit) and manual review without functional test execution.
Missing_Evidence: Functional correctness test-suite verification; real-world repository CVE evaluation.

Study_Title: Repairing Regex Vulnerabilities via Localization-Guided Instructions
M1_Justification: Decouples symbolic vulnerability localization (pinpointing exact ReDoS sub-patterns) from constrained LLM patch synthesis with multi-step logical repair instructions in Localized Regex Repair (LRR) (Abstract, Section 7).
M2_Justification: Verifies repaired regexes across three complementary dimensions: dynamic ReDoS elimination via ReDoSHunter (1-minute attack timeout), syntactic preservation (RLI and Normalized Levenshtein Similarity), and semantic equivalence (Jaccard similarity over generated strings) (Sections 5.2.1–5.2.3).
M3_Justification: Evaluates LRR across five LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-oss-20B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma3-12B, Phi4-14B) against symbolic SOTA baseline RegexScalpel, achieving +15.4 pp repair gain with semantic-similarity trade-off curves (Abstract, Fig. 1).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases open-source code on GitHub (https://github.com/cdltlehf/LRR) and supports multiple open-weight and frontier LLMs, though specialized exclusively to regex ReDoS vulnerabilities (Abstract, Limitations).
Key_Strengths: Symbolic sub-pattern localization + LLM repair; joint dynamic ReDoS attack testing (ReDoSHunter) and semantic equivalence checks; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Narrowly scoped to ReDoS vulnerabilities in regular expressions; relies on heuristic anti-patterns and empirical 1-minute fuzzing timeouts.
Missing_Evidence: Formal regex equivalence guarantees; broader CWE scope beyond ReDoS; bibliographic year/venue metadata.

Study_Title: PSearch: Search-Based Patch Generation in the Era of LLM-Based Automated Program Repair
M1_Justification: Implements a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided iterative patch generation and refinement framework combining CoT patch generation, automated test execution feedback, LLM reward scoring, and search-state backpropagation (Abstract, Algorithm 1).
M2_Justification: Runs automated test suites at every MCTS search step to filter plausible patches and performs manual semantic equivalence/correctness validation against developer ground-truth fixes upon search completion (Algorithm 1, Page 5).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked across five datasets (835 Defects4J bugs: 201 fixed; 79 real-world Java vulnerabilities in VUL4J: 27 fixed; 300 SWE-Bench-Lite issues: 164 resolved; QuixBugs; ConDefects) against 12 SOTA baselines with ablations and >50% cost reduction analysis (Abstract, Sections 4.1–4.2, 7).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases code, scripts, data, and results on GitHub (https://github.com/Tomsawyerhu/Psearch), handles multi-language repository issues (Java and Python), and cuts inference costs by >50% (Section 7, Data Availability).
Key_Strengths: Principled MCTS search-state management with execution feedback; strong vulnerability (27/79 VUL4J) and repository-level (164/300 SWE-Bench-Lite) results; >50% cost reduction; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Potential pre-training memorization on public benchmarks; stochastic LLM/MCTS variance; manual correctness check required post-search.
Missing_Evidence: Dedicated post-patch exploit/sanitizer security checks beyond benchmark test suites; formal venue/year metadata.

Study_Title: On the Evaluation of Large Language Models in Multilingual Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Applies Tree-sitter AST parsing for vulnerable function extraction and evaluates instruction-tuned and prompted LLMs in a sequence-to-sequence setup (Section 4.2, Page 31), lacking SAST/DAST feedback loops or automated CI/CD integration.
M2_Justification: Evaluates patches exclusively via static match-based metrics (Exact Match, BLEU, ROUGE) supplemented by manual failure inspection of selected cases (Section 7, Page 31), without compilation, unit test suites, or dynamic exploit execution.
M3_Justification: Conducts a large-scale multilingual benchmark across seven programming languages (C, C#, C++, Go, JavaScript, Java, Python) comparing five SOTA LLMs, four prompting/tuning strategies, and fine-tuned AVR baselines (VulMaster, CodeT5), including unseen-language generalization tests (Abstract, Section 4, Fig. 5).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the full replication package (data and source code) on the project homepage and covers seven programming languages across high-severity vulnerabilities (Abstract, Section 8).
Key_Strengths: Broad 7-language empirical evaluation; tests cross-language generalization on unseen languages; benchmarks frontier LLMs against VulMaster/CodeT5; public replication package.
Limitations: Relies strictly on static match metrics (EM, BLEU, ROUGE) without compilation or dynamic execution testing; fault localization identified as a key bottleneck.
Missing_Evidence: Execution-based or PoC security verification of generated patches; DOI metadata.

Study_Title: TerraRepair: A Tool-Grounded LLM Agent for Infrastructure-As-Code Repair
M1_Justification: Implements a bounded ReAct tool-grounded agent integrating Terraform dependency-graph retrieval, installed provider-schema lookup, in-loop Checkov/Trivy scanner verification, and structured escalation for missing deployment context (Abstract, Section 3, Fig. 1).
M2_Justification: Verifies patches via dual static security scanners (Checkov and Trivy), terraform validate syntax/schema checks, and a majority-vote semantic audit by two LLM judges and one author confirming 78.9% semantic correctness on AWS repairs (Abstract, Section 4, Table 2).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across two vulnerable-by-design Terraform repositories (TerraGoat and KaiMonkey) spanning AWS, Azure, and GCP against a controlled one-shot baseline across three runs, restricted to synthetic IaC repositories rather than production multi-module codebases (Abstract, Section 4, Table 2).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the full replication package, tool interfaces, evaluation scripts, and semantic-audit artifacts on GitHub (https://github.com/ManassehV2/TerraRepair) and incorporates structured human escalation for unresolved secrets/policies (Sections 1, 3, 4).
Key_Strengths: Closed-loop ReAct agent combining provider schemas, dependency graphs, and Checkov/Trivy re-scans; slashes claimed-vs-verified repair gap to <5 pp; public GitHub replication package.
Limitations: Evaluated only on vulnerable-by-design benchmarks (TerraGoat, KaiMonkey) with semantic audit restricted to AWS; validation errors on Azure/GCP due to missing external references.
Missing_Evidence: Evaluation on real-world production Terraform repositories; automated runtime cloud deployment/plan verification.

Study_Title: SCPatcher: Automated Smart Contract Code Repair via Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Knowledge Graph
M1_Justification: Integrates Slither static analysis to extract Solidity entity-relationship triples into a Neo4j/NetworkX knowledge graph, CodeBERT dense embeddings with multi-stage structure-aware reranking, two-stage RAG + CoT repair, and iterative Slither verification (Abstract, Section 3, Fig. 1).
M2_Justification: Verifies patches via Solidity compilation checks (91.0% pass rate) and Slither static re-verification (81.5% repair rate across 200 contracts), without dynamic EVM exploit transactions, fuzzing, or unit test execution (Abstract, Section 3, Table 1).
M3_Justification: Evaluates on 200 vulnerable Solidity smart contracts against three prompting baselines (DirectFix, LogicRepair, SelfRefine) plus ablations, scoped to a single domain/language (Solidity) and 200 contracts without dynamic behavioral tests (Section 4, Tables 1–2).
M4_Justification: Targets pre-deployment Solidity smart contract auditing with measured GPU runtime, but provides no public GitHub/Zenodo artifact URL or CI/CD deployment integration in the manuscript (Sections 1, 4).
Key_Strengths: Combines Slither-extracted contract knowledge graphs, multi-stage clone-deduplicated reranking, and two-stage CoT refinement achieving 81.5% static repair rate.
Limitations: Relies solely on Slither static analysis for verification (risking detector overfitting without functional/dynamic exploit tests); limited to single-contract patterns; no public code repository.
Missing_Evidence: Public replication artifact repository; dynamic exploit/unit test execution validation; peer-reviewed venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: RegoMender: A Multi-agent Framework for Automated Rego Policy Repair
M1_Justification: Coordinates three specialized agents (Orchestrator, Analyzer, Repairer) via a shared Blackboard and a deterministic five-operation atomic toolkit (Verify via opa check/opa test, Context Scan, Error Triage, Rewrite, Patch) with rollback support (Abstract, Sections 1, 3.2).
M2_Justification: Validates every patch using dual automated OPA verification—syntactic/type compilation checks (opa check, 82.9%) and executable policy unit test suites (opa test, 77.9% semantic pass rate)—plus real-world CVE validation (Abstract, Section 3).
M3_Justification: Constructs and evaluates on RegoBench (1,159 real-world defects across 7 defect types from 2,847 GitHub repositories), tests single-step and chained multi-error repairs, and demonstrates cross-language generalization on HCL and 132 real-world CVEs (86.4% fix rate) (Abstract, Sections 3.1, 4).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the RegoBench dataset, RegoMender implementation, and execution traces via Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19230997) and directly targets CI/CD and Kubernetes admission-control OPA pipelines (Sections 1, 5).
Key_Strengths: Large-scale real-world benchmark (1,159 Rego defects + 132 CVEs); closed-loop multi-agent blackboard architecture with rollback and opa check/test execution; cross-language generalization to HCL/SQL; public Zenodo artifacts.
Limitations: Bounded iteration limits can stall on deeply coupled multi-error policy chains; mined GitHub commits may occasionally bundle non-security refactoring.
Missing_Evidence: Live Kubernetes admission-controller latency and production CI/CD deployment telemetry.

Study_Title: Identifying Helpful Context for LLM-based Vulnerability Repair: A Preliminary Study
M1_Justification: Builds an automated patch-insertion and test-runner harness around Vul4J to evaluate zero-shot GPT-4o/GPT-4 across nine prompt variants, though repository code context is manually extracted rather than retrieved via automated static/dynamic tools (Abstract, Sections 1, 3.1).
M2_Justification: Validates generated patches automatically inside Vul4J using Maven/Gradle compilation, functional regression test suites, and Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) exploit tests across three repeated runs per prompt (Abstract, Section 3.1, Table 1).
M3_Justification: Evaluates 10 prompt configurations across 3 runs (30 runs total) on 42 reproducible Java vulnerabilities from Vul4J, restricted to a single language (Java), small sample size (42 CVEs), and two OpenAI models (GPT-4 and GPT-4o) (Abstract, Sections 3, 5).
M4_Justification: Releases prompts and experimental artifacts on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15036666), but relies on manual code context extraction and requires manual Java-version environment fixes, precluding turnkey deployment (Sections 1, 3.1).
Key_Strengths: Rigorous multi-run Vul4J execution validation; isolates impact of CVE descriptions, CWE metadata, and repository context; public Zenodo replication package.
Limitations: Manual extraction of repository context introduces subjectivity; limited to 42 Java vulnerabilities and GPT-4/GPT-4o; lacks semantic equivalence auditing beyond PoV/unit tests.
Missing_Evidence: Automated context-retrieval pipeline; multi-language evaluation; valid DOI metadata.

Study_Title: Security Weaknesses of Copilot-Generated Code in GitHub Projects: An Empirical Study
Venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
M1_Justification: Feeds static analysis diagnostic warnings (Bandit, CodeQL, ESLint security plugins) into Copilot Chat to evaluate interactive vulnerability remediation of AI-generated snippets, without automated closed-loop verification or autonomous tool orchestration (Abstract, Sections 1, 3).
M2_Justification: Verifies Copilot Chat fixes by re-running static analyzers (Bandit, CodeQL, ESLint) combined with manual author inspection of CWE classifications and fixes (up to 55.5% repair rate), without dynamic exploit PoCs or project unit test execution (Abstract, Section 3).
M3_Justification: Analyzes 733 real-world AI-generated snippets (GitHub Copilot, CodeWhisperer, Codeium) mined from open-source GitHub repositories across Python and JavaScript spanning 43 CWE categories (including CWE Top-25) and evaluates remediation across tool warnings (Abstract, Sections 3–4, Table 5).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the dataset and analysis artifacts on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10802054) and provides actionable developer mitigation guidelines, though remediation relies on manual developer prompting in Copilot Chat (Abstract, Section 1).
Key_Strengths: Large-scale empirical mining of 733 real-world AI-generated code snippets across 43 CWEs in Python and JavaScript; evaluates SAST-guided Copilot Chat repair; public Zenodo dataset.
Limitations: Repair evaluation relies on static analyzer re-scans and manual review rather than executable test suites or exploit PoCs; interactive Copilot Chat workflow is not automated.
Missing_Evidence: Dynamic functional regression and exploit validation of repaired snippets; final published TOSEM DOI.

Study_Title: APPATCH: Automated Adaptive Prompting Large Language Models for Real-World Software Vulnerability Patching
M1_Justification: Uses Joern static code analysis to construct System Dependence Graphs (SDGs) and extract interprocedural backward slices via semantics-aware scoping, paired with multi-step vulnerability semantics reasoning and adaptive prompting across LLMs (Abstract, Sections 1, 4).
M2_Justification: Evaluates patches on ExtractFix via test/exploit recall and on 306+76+20 real-world/zero-day C samples using structured semantic equivalence and vulnerability-elimination criteria against ground-truth patches, as most zero-day samples lack compilable harnesses or PoCs (Abstract, Sections 1, 5).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across 97 zero-day vulnerabilities (306+76 samples) and 20 ExtractFix CVEs across four frontier/open LLMs (GPT-4, Claude-3.5, Gemini-1.5, Llama-3.1), comparing against prompting baselines and non-LLM tools (ExtractFix, VulnFix) with time and dollar cost analysis (Abstract, Sections 5–6, Table 5).
M4_Justification: Releases full source code, datasets, documentation, and experimental results on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/14741018), operates on uncompilable code without requiring PoCs/training, and achieves $0.0026–$0.0823 per-patch cost (Sections 1, 6, Data Availability).
Key_Strengths: Joern SDG interprocedural backward slicing works on uncompilable code without PoCs or fine-tuning; strong evaluation on 97 zero-day vulnerabilities and ExtractFix; detailed latency/token cost metrics; public Zenodo release.
Limitations: Limited to C/C++ codebases; zero-day evaluation relies on manual/ground-truth patch comparison rather than automated runtime exploit and regression test execution.
Missing_Evidence: Automated dynamic functional/exploit test validation across all evaluated zero-day cases; cross-language evaluation.

Study_Title: Applying generative artificial intelligence for vulnerability fixing in a proprietary software ecosystem
M1_Justification: Develops PSECO-SafePatch, a web-based remediation tool integrating Fortify Static Code Analyzer (.ear and .sarif ingestion) with GenAI patch generation, structured remediation wizards, Jira/Bitbucket/Bamboo CI/CD workflow integration, and human-in-the-loop verification gates (Abstract, Section 5).
M2_Justification: Validates the system through an industrial participative case study combining Fortify static re-verification, structured human-in-the-loop developer approval gates, and a survey evaluation (PEoU/PU) of 18 enterprise developers and technical leads, without automated dynamic exploit testing (Abstract, Sections 5, 7).
M3_Justification: Evaluates within a single large global proprietary software ecosystem (PSECO) with 18 practitioners rather than multi-project open-source benchmarks or cross-model quantitative baselines (Abstract, Section 7, Table 6).
M4_Justification: Directly deployed and evaluated inside a real enterprise CI/CD ecosystem (Fortify, Jira, Bitbucket, Bamboo) under regulatory governance and publicly releases prototype source code and evaluation instruments on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15386005) (Abstract, Sections 5, 7).
Key_Strengths: Rare industrial participative case study in a real proprietary software ecosystem; end-to-end SARIF/Fortify + CI/CD integration with governance guardrails; public Zenodo prototype.
Limitations: Single-organization case study with 18 survey participants; lacks automated dynamic PoC/regression testing and multi-LLM benchmark comparisons.
Missing_Evidence: Automated functional regression and dynamic security test pass rates across a standardized CVE corpus.

Study_Title: Can You Really Trust Code Copilots? Evaluating Large Language Models from a Code Security Perspective
M1_Justification: Constructs the CoV-Eval multi-task evaluation harness and fine-tunes VC-Judge (on Llama3-8B-Instruct) to automate security review of LLM-generated/repaired code, though vulnerability repair itself is evaluated via single-turn inference without static/dynamic tool feedback loops (Abstract, Sections 3, 5).
M2_Justification: Evaluates repair via the Security Rate (SR) metric judged by VC-Judge (validated for alignment with human security experts) alongside HumanEval pass@1 usability correlation, without project-level compilation, unit test suites, or dynamic PoC exploit execution (Abstract, Sections 3.4, 5, Table 5).
M3_Justification: Benchmarks 20 proprietary and open-source LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3, DeepSeek-V2, Llama 3, Qwen 2, CodeLlama, WizardCoder, etc.) across multi-task dimensions (code completion, vulnerability repair, detection, and CWE classification) with human-alignment validation (Abstract, Sections 5–6, Tables 1, 5).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the CoV-Eval dataset, VC-Judge model/code, and evaluation harness on GitHub (https://github.com/MurrayTom/CoV-Eval), though intended as an offline benchmark rather than a production repair tool (Section 1, Footnote 1).
Key_Strengths: Comprehensive 20-LLM benchmark spanning repair, secure generation, and detection; introduces human-aligned VC-Judge evaluator; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Relies on LLM-as-a-judge (VC-Judge) rather than deterministic compiler/PoC/regression test execution for repair verification; single-inference prompting without iterative tool feedback.
Missing_Evidence: Execution-based compilation, unit test, and PoC exploit verification for repaired code; peer-reviewed venue/DOI.

Study_Title: LLMs in Code Vulnerability Analysis: A Proof of Concept
Venue: SVM 2026 (Fourth International Workshop on Software Vulnerability Management)
M1_Justification: Evaluates standalone open-source LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, and QLoRA/fine-tuning regimes directly on Big-Vul and VulRepair snippets without static analyzers, compilers, dynamic executors, or agentic tool loops (Abstract, Sections 3–4).
M2_Justification: Evaluates vulnerability repair solely with static text/token similarity metrics (CodeBLEU, CodeBERTScore, BLEU, ChrF) against ground-truth commits, explicitly noting metric discrepancies and performing no compilation, unit test, or PoC exploit execution (Abstract, Sections 4, 7).
M3_Justification: Systematically compares 10 open-source LLMs (five code-specific vs. general-purpose pairs including DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen, Mistral, Llama, Gemma) across zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning settings on Big-Vul and VulRepair for detection, severity prediction, and repair (Abstract, Sections 3–5, Tables 2–6).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the codebase and processed dataset on Figshare (https://figshare.com/s/a06ec09cd1bd98e6dd45) and demonstrates resource-efficient fine-tuning on commodity GPUs, though lacking execution validation for deployment readiness (Sections 1, 7).
Key_Strengths: Controlled paired comparison of 5 code-specific vs. 5 general-purpose open-source LLMs across zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned regimes; public Figshare artifact release.
Limitations: Relies exclusively on non-executable lexical metrics (BLEU, CodeBLEU, CodeBERTScore, ChrF) for patch evaluation; C/C++ function-level snippets only.
Missing_Evidence: Compilation, functional test suite, and dynamic security/PoC verification of generated patches; final ACM DOI.

Study_Title: A Case Study of LLM for Automated Vulnerability Repair: Assessing Impact of Reasoning and Patch Validation Feedback
Venue: AIware 2024 (1st ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software)
M1_Justification: Implements VRpilot, an iterative repair pipeline combining Chain-of-Thought vulnerability reasoning with an automated feedback loop driven by external compilers, code sanitizers (ASAN, UBSAN), and functional test suites (Abstract, Sections 1, 2).
M2_Justification: Validates patches against both security specifications (ASAN/UBSAN sanitizer exploit checks) and functional specifications (project test suites) to filter plausible patches, supplemented by manual correctness comparison against reference developer patches (Abstract, Sections 2.1, 3, 5.2).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across both C (ExtractFix) and Java (Vul4J) benchmarks against CodexVR and state-of-the-art APR/AVR baselines with 50 samples per bug and systematic ablation studies isolating CoT reasoning and tool validation feedback (Abstract, Sections 3–4, Table 3).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the replication package (http://tinyurl.com/vrpilot-artifacts) and demonstrates cross-language C/Java applicability, though evaluated with GPT-3.5 on established benchmarks with manual inspection for final correctness (Sections 1, 3.1, 5.2).
Key_Strengths: Closed-loop CoT reasoning + compiler/sanitizer (ASAN/UBSAN)/test feedback; dual-language C and Java validation; rigorous ablation studies; public artifact package.
Limitations: Evaluated primarily with GPT-3.5 using 50-sample querying; plausible patches still require manual inspection against developer patches to rule out overfitting.
Missing_Evidence: Evaluation on newer frontier/open-weight LLMs and multi-file repository vulnerabilities.

Study_Title: A Study of Vulnerability Repair in JavaScript Programs with Large Language Models
Venue: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2024 (WWW '24 Companion)
M1_Justification: Evaluates black-box conversational LLMs (ChatGPT and Bard) using manual prompt templates containing vulnerability names, descriptions, and CWE context without static analyzers, compilers, or automated feedback loops (Abstract, Section 3).
M2_Justification: Validates generated JavaScript patches by executing functional/security test cases and manual inspection of correctness across prompt variants, without automated SAST/DAST or fuzzing pipelines (Abstract, Section 4.3).
M3_Justification: Evaluates two commercial LLMs (ChatGPT and Bard) on real-world JavaScript CWE vulnerabilities (including CWE Top-25 items such as CWE-20, CWE-22, CWE-77), limited to a single language and small benchmark scale (Abstract, Section 4, Table 1).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases repair prompts and testing results on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10783763), though relying on interactive web interfaces (ChatGPT/Bard) without automated CI/CD or IDE integration (Section 1, Footnote 1).
Key_Strengths: Early empirical investigation of LLM-based vulnerability repair in dynamic JavaScript code across CWE Top-25 classes; quantifies prompt-context sensitivity; public Zenodo artifact.
Limitations: Manual black-box prompting via ChatGPT/Bard web interfaces; small JavaScript sample size; lacks automated static/dynamic feedback loops or model fine-tuning.
Missing_Evidence: Automated execution-based SAST/exploit verification pipeline; evaluation on modern open-weight/frontier code models.

Study_Title: How Effective Are Neural Networks for Fixing Security Vulnerabilities
Venue: ISSTA 2023 (32nd ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis)
M1_Justification: Integrates AST/identifier code simplification transformations (src2abs) and automated test-harness execution for top-10 candidate patches across LLMs and DL-based APR models, assuming perfect fault localization without static/dynamic tool feedback loops (Abstract, Sections 5, 5.1).
M2_Justification: Validates every generated patch through project compilation, automated security/functional test suites in Vul4J and VJBench, and manual inspection of all test-passing plausible patches to distinguish true semantic fixes from overfitted patches (Abstract, Sections 5, 6).
M3_Justification: Evaluates 5 pre-trained LLMs (Codex, CodeGen, CodeT5, PLBART, InCoder), 4 fine-tuned LLMs, and 4 DL-based APR models across 50 real-world single-hunk Java CVEs in Vul4J and the newly curated VJBench plus data-leakage-controlled VJBench-trans (Abstract, Sections 5–6, Table 4).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the VJBench benchmark, code transformation scripts, and replication artifacts on GitHub (https://github.com/lin-tan/llm-vul), though restricted to single-hunk Java bugs with assumed perfect fault localization (Section 5.1, References [5]).
Key_Strengths: First systematic comparison of LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and DL-APR on Java vulnerabilities; introduces VJBench and leakage-controlled VJBench-trans; dual test + manual patch validation; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Restricted to 50 single-hunk Java vulnerabilities with assumed perfect fault localization; older 2022–2023 model cohort (Codex, CodeT5, PLBART).
Missing_Evidence: Multi-hunk/multi-file vulnerability repair; end-to-end fault localization without oracle line hints.

Study_Title: LLMSecCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Secure Coding
M1_Justification: Builds a modular open-source evaluation harness integrating HuggingFace model loaders, customizable chat templates, correction-chain prompts, and CyberSecEval test runners for local open-source LLMs, though without interactive static/dynamic analysis feedback loops (Abstract, Sections 2, 3).
M2_Justification: Executes automated unit/security test suites (pass@1 and pass rates) and CyberSecEval static/rule checks via eval_code, alongside cross-actor consistency checks (5% delta), without manual semantic equivalence auditing (Abstract, Sections 1.4, 3).
M3_Justification: Evaluates parameter and prompt sensitivity (10% and 9% performance variance) across secure code generation and automated program repair tasks using open-source models and CyberSecEval benchmarks, though limited in model breadth and real-world CVE depth (Abstract, Sections 1–3).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the full open-source framework and evaluation data on GitHub (https://github.com/anton-ryden/LLMSecCode) with plug-and-play HuggingFace local model support eliminating paid API dependencies (Abstract, Section 1.4, Section 2).
Key_Strengths: Open-source, locally deployable HuggingFace evaluation framework extending CyberSecEval to local open-weight models; quantifies prompt and hyperparameter sensitivity; public GitHub repository.
Limitations: Primarily a benchmark/evaluation harness rather than a novel repair architecture; limited evaluation scale across real-world multi-file CVEs; preprint status.
Missing_Evidence: Large-scale evaluation on real-world CVE datasets with paired functional and exploit tests; peer-reviewed venue/DOI.

Study_Title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
M1_Justification: Equips an autonomous coding agent (Claude Code with Haiku 4.5) with five on-demand static program-analysis map tools (AST via tree-sitter, Call Graph via Jedi, Module Dependencies, Documentation-enriched search via Griffe, and a Hybrid tool) alongside native execution tools (Abstract, Sections I, III).
M2_Justification: Validates generated patches via automated Dockerized execution test harnesses—hidden fail-to-pass exploit/reproducer tests and pass-to-pass regression suites on SecBench and SWE-bench Pro—supplemented by manual trajectory failure-mode categorization (Abstract, Section IV, Fig. 2).
M3_Justification: Conducts a controlled cross-representation study across four repository-level benchmarks—SecBench (security patching), SWE-bench Pro (program repair), LinuxFLBench (fault localization), and SWT-bench (test generation)—measuring resolution rate, token usage, tool calls, and wall-clock latency (Abstract, Section IV).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the experiment harness, representation tools, and metrics scripts on GitHub (https://github.com/MelikaSepidband/How-Should-Agents-See-Code), though evaluated with a single backbone model (Claude Haiku 4.5) and noting higher wall-clock latency (Abstract, Section II, Section VI).
Key_Strengths: Controlled empirical comparison of 5 code-representation tools (AST, Call Graph, Dependencies, Docs, Hybrid) inside a repository-level agent on SecBench and SWE-bench Pro; quantifies token-cost vs. latency trade-offs; public GitHub artifact.
Limitations: Evaluated only with Claude Haiku 4.5; non-code configuration files (YAML, docker-compose) bypass code maps; map queries increase wall-clock latency.
Missing_Evidence: Multi-model evaluation across frontier and open-weight agent backbones; peer-reviewed venue/DOI metadata.
Evidence_Location: Abstract; Sections I, II, IV, VI; Fig. 2 (Pages 1–6)

Study_Title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Implements a closed-loop generative adversarial multi-agent system where an Exploitation Agent synthesizes reproducing Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) inputs, a Patching Agent repairs the codebase, and the Exploitation Agent iteratively attacks each candidate patch to accumulate bypass PoVs until all are blocked (Abstract, Sections 1, 3).
M2_Justification: Enforces strict separation between construction-time PoVs and held-out evaluation security oracles alongside project-specific build checks, sanitizer traces, and regression test suites to eliminate oracle-reuse overfitting (Abstract, Sections 1, 5, 6).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across 101 real-world CVEs (60 Java and 41 C/C++) spanning 61 repositories and 20 CWE classes on VulnRepairBench under strict leakage controls, comparing against single-pass Claude Code and state-of-the-art agentic repair systems across multiple models (Abstract, Sections 5–6, Table 2).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the full orchestration code, container definitions, agent prompts, and scoring scripts on GitHub (https://github.com/P2Patch/P2patch) with pinned containerized execution contracts and detailed cost/runtime accounting (Section 5, Open Science).
Key_Strengths: Novel adversarial exploit-vs-patch hardening loop exposing bypasses in 41% of initially plausible patches; strict held-out security oracle separation; 101 Java and C/C++ CVEs across 61 repos; public GitHub artifact.
Limitations: Higher compute/token cost due to multi-round adversarial PoV synthesis; requires reproducible containerized build and execution contracts.
Missing_Evidence: Formal peer-reviewed publication venue and DOI metadata.

Study_Title: The History Is the Detector: Executing CVE Patch History, End-to-End
M1_Justification: Implements BUGSTONE-E2E, a funnel-shaped hybrid pipeline combining deterministic Tree-sitter AST call-site enumeration and heuristic pruning with multi-agent LLM inspection, runtime exploit verification, and scope-checked patch generation across multiple coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Pi) (Abstract, Sections 1, 5.1).
M2_Justification: Validates both findings and generated patches via runtime exploit confirmation and two-sided differential testing comparing pre-patch and post-patch execution behavior (Abstract, Section 5).
M3_Justification: Mines 19,325 high-severity CVEs (2022–2026) to synthesize 1,033 rules across 56 CWE families (172 skills), evaluates across 14 real-world programs (producing 644 runtime-verified findings), and benchmarks multiple LLMs (GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Kimi-K2.5) and three external security harnesses (Abstract, Sections 5–6, Table 2).
M4_Justification: Designed as a scalable, cost-tiered industrial security-scanning and remediation pipeline at IBM Research with explicit reproducibility and cost measurements, though no public GitHub/Zenodo artifact URL is provided in the manuscript (Abstract, Sections 5, 7.1).
Key_Strengths: End-to-end CVE-history-to-detection-and-repair funnel combining deterministic Tree-sitter pruning with agentic reasoning and two-sided differential runtime verification; large-scale 19,325-CVE mining and multi-harness evaluation.
Limitations: Scoped to recurring operation/API-anchored flaws rather than global stateful invariants; runtime confirmation requires reproducible build environments; no public code repository link.
Missing_Evidence: Publicly accessible source code/skill repository URL; formal peer-reviewed venue/DOI.

Study_Title: CyberFactory: Scaling Cyber Security Capabilities with Instances from the Wild
M1_Justification: Builds an automated environment-reconstruction and agentic trajectory-synthesis pipeline integrating git history extraction, sanitizer instrumentation, tool-using agent rollouts, and trajectory-trained OpenAegis models for PoC generation, vulnerability patching, and CyberQA (Abstract, Sections 1, 3, Fig. 2).
M2_Justification: Enforces two-sided differential runtime verification V(x) = CRASH(b-, x) ∧ ¬CRASH(b+, x) using sanitizer instrumentation across pre-patch and post-patch builds alongside functional regression preservation (Abstract, Sections 3, 4.1, Fig. 1).
M3_Justification: Synthesizes difficulty-calibrated instances from ARVO, OSS-Fuzz, and wild CVEs across PoC generation, vulnerability patching, and CyberQA, evaluating OpenAegis against general-purpose open-weight and closed-source backbones on CyberGym (achieving 58.1% Pass@1, +28.5 points over Qwen 3.5) (Abstract, Sections 3–4).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases both the synthesized dataset on HuggingFace (Multilingual-Multimodal-NLP/cyberfactory) and the framework/model training pipeline on GitHub (https://github.com/CSJianYang/CyberFactory) with internalized skill execution requiring no inference-time skill overhead (Abstract, Page 1, Footnote 2).
Key_Strengths: Unified open-source data-synthesis and agentic RL/SFT training framework with two-sided sanitizer differential verification; trains OpenAegis (+28.5 Pass@1 over Qwen 3.5); public GitHub and HuggingFace releases.
Limitations: Focuses primarily on C/C++ sanitizer-instrumented OSS-Fuzz/ARVO/CVE targets; dual-use safety considerations noted for PoC synthesis.
Missing_Evidence: Formal peer-reviewed publication venue and DOI metadata; evaluation on non-memory-safety web/cloud languages.

Study_Title: Vul4Py: Benchmarking Automated Vulnerability Repair in Python with Paired Exploit and Functional Oracles
M1_Justification: Constructs a reproducible containerized execution and paired-oracle validation harness comparing a static-slicing specialized tool (APPATCH), directly prompted LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4), and autonomous SWE agents (OpenHands, Trae Agent, SWE-agent) under uniform step/cost budgets (Abstract, Sections 4.1–4.2).
M2_Justification: Requires every candidate patch to pass a strict paired oracle—an exploit test that fails on the vulnerable revision and passes on the patched code plus the full project-native pytest functional regression suite—supplemented by manual semantic-equivalence inspection against developer patches (98/104 confirmed equivalent) (Abstract, Sections 4.1, 5.1).
M3_Justification: Curates 100 real-world Python vulnerabilities across 60 open-source projects and 60 distinct CWEs (2017–2025) and systematically evaluates six distinct approaches across three paradigms, reporting resolution rates, false-positive exploit-only filtering, token cost, and wall-clock runtime (Abstract, Sections 4–5, Table 2).
