M4_Justification: Publicly releases the complete Vul4Py benchmark, pinned per-instance environments, and evaluation pipeline on GitHub (https://github.com/tabudz/vul4py) with empirical per-instance cost ($1.32–$7.52) and latency metrics (Abstract, Section 5.1, Data Availability).
Key_Strengths: 100 reproducible real-world Python CVEs across 60 projects/CWEs with paired exploit + pytest regression oracles and manual semantic verification; exposes 5x–10x superiority of agentic loops over one-shot LLMs; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Limited to Python repositories; evaluated primarily with proprietary frontier backbones (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4) rather than open-weight models.
Missing_Evidence: Evaluation on open-weight agent backbones; peer-reviewed venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: Does Runtime Topology Context Improve LLM-Generated Kubernetes Security Patches?
M1_Justification: Develops KuTIE (Kubernetes Topology Intelligence Engine), which extracts live runtime service-call graphs from Istio telemetry, Trivy KSPM findings, and Kubernetes service-account RBAC/Secret/ConfigMap bindings to condition LLM security patch synthesis (Abstract, Sections 1, 4.2).
M2_Justification: Validates patches against live cluster ground truth across a 36-deployment, 4-namespace Kubernetes cluster by verifying both security remediation against four end-to-end exploit chains (C1–C4) and preservation of all 51 directed runtime service-call edges without functional blast-radius breakage (Abstract, Sections 4.2, 6.1).
M3_Justification: Executes 248 controlled trials crossing 31 injectable KSPM findings (25 topology-dependent, 6 topology-independent controls) across 7 dependency classes and 4 frontier/open-weight models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large), demonstrating a +66.9 pp correctness gain (11.1% to 78.0%) (Abstract, Section 6.1).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases both the VulnCare Kubernetes testbed (https://github.com/dynatrace-research/vulncare) and the KuTIE evaluation framework and results (https://github.com/dynatrace-research/kutie-artifacts), grounded in production Dynatrace/Istio/Trivy observability primitives (Page 7 Footnote 1, Section 1).
Key_Strengths: Live Kubernetes/Istio runtime topology context prevents destructive functional blast radius in KSPM remediation (+66.9 pp gain); validated on live 36-deployment cluster with 4 exploit chains and topology-independent controls; dual public GitHub repositories.
Limitations: Single-turn evaluation on a synthetic healthcare cluster (31 findings); requires active service-mesh (Istio) telemetry.
Missing_Evidence: Multi-turn iterative cluster rollout verification; peer-reviewed venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: Bulkhead: Automated Semantic Detection and Remediation of Container Escape Vulnerabilities
M1_Justification: Implements an end-to-end semantic detection and remediation pipeline that mines historical CVEs into structured patterns, recovers source-to-sink host-container execution contexts, generates repository-specific patches, checks builds, and iteratively verifies path safety via SPIN-based bounded model checking before runtime PoC replay (Abstract, Section 5, Appendix A).
M2_Justification: Validates generated patches across three distinct layers—repository compilation/test suites, SPIN formal bounded model checking templates with counterexample refinement, and isolated runtime PoC exploit replay—and submitted verified patches upstream resulting in 3 assigned CVEs (Abstract, Section 5, Appendix A).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across 82 mainstream container repositories (discovering 20 zero-day path-traversal vulnerabilities, 43% of the decade baseline) plus a leakage-controlled benchmark of 25 post-cutoff CVEs (post-September 2024) with component ablation studies (Abstract, Sections 5.1, 7).
M4_Justification: Demonstrates real-world upstream impact with 20 zero-day discoveries, 3 newly assigned CVEs, and maintainer-submitted verified patches across production container toolkits, though no public GitHub/Zenodo code link is listed in the paper (Abstract, Section 7).
Key_Strengths: Combines LLM patch generation with formal SPIN bounded model checking and runtime PoC replay; discovered 20 real-world zero-days across 82 container repositories with 3 CVEs assigned and upstream patches submitted; strict post-cutoff leakage control.
Limitations: Specialized to container host-boundary path traversal logic flaws; runtime replay depends on reconstructible container build environments; no public artifact repository link.
Missing_Evidence: Public artifact/code release URL; formal publication venue and DOI metadata.

Study_Title: RAVEN: Agentic RAG for Automated Vulnerability Repair
M1_Justification: Combines historical vulnerability-fix RAG retrieval with a dedicated Curator Agent extracting cross-file repository dependencies and a controlled iterative repair-verification loop (Abstract, Sections 1, 6).
M2_Justification: Verifies candidate patches via automated execution-based testing and structured iterative feedback inside containerized environments across C and Java benchmarks rather than lexical similarity (Abstract, Section 4).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked across 160 real-world CVEs spanning C and Java, 10+ CWE families, unseen CWEs, and out-of-distribution settings, achieving 83.13% repair success (Abstract, Section 4.1, Table 1).
M4_Justification: Engineered for local, low-cost execution on commodity GPUs using medium open-weight LLMs (Gemma-4-26B, Nemotron), though omitting a public GitHub repository URL in the manuscript (Abstract, Section 1).
Key_Strengths: Cross-file Curator Agent + historical-fix RAG with iterative execution verification; dual-language C and Java evaluation on 160 CVEs including unseen CWEs; local open-weight execution.
Limitations: No public artifact/GitHub URL in the paper; performance relies on historical fix corpus coverage.
Missing_Evidence: Public code/artifact repository link; formal publication venue and DOI metadata.

Study_Title: VulKey: Automated Vulnerability Repair Guided by Domain-Specific Repair Patterns
Venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), Vol. 3, No. FSE, Article FSE110
M1_Justification: Pairs hierarchical CWE/syntactic-action/semantic-key-element pattern extraction and context-aware pattern selection with a two-phase fine-tuned LLM, assuming pre-localized bug markers and CWE labels without closed-loop compiler/PoC feedback (Abstract, Section 4.1).
M2_Justification: Evaluates C/C++ PrimeVul patches using exact/semantic match against developer fixes and Java Vul4J patches using execution-based test validation, acknowledging the absence of runtime verification on PrimeVul (Abstract, Sections 5, 6.2).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked on large-scale C/C++ PrimeVul (31.5% accuracy, +7.6% over VulMaster and GPT-5) and cross-language Java Vul4J, supported by ablations, pattern audits, and data-leakage controls (Abstract, Sections 5.1, 6.2).
M4_Justification: Achieves polynomial-time O(n) pattern matching and strong open-weight performance (StarCoder), though requiring pre-marked //bug_start regions and two-phase fine-tuning without a public repository link (Sections 4.1, 5, 6.2).
Key_Strengths: Published in PACMSE/FSE 2026; interpretable three-level security repair patterns outperforming VulMaster and GPT-5 on PrimeVul; cross-language validation on Vul4J.
Limitations: Requires pre-localized buggy regions and CWE labels; PrimeVul evaluation relies on static reference matching rather than dynamic PoC/test execution; no public code link.
Missing_Evidence: Execution-based PoC and regression test validation on C/C++ PrimeVul; public replication repository link.

Study_Title: Why LLMs Fail: A Failure Analysis and Partial Success Measurement for Automated Security Patch Generation
M1_Justification: Builds a tri-axis evaluation pipeline integrating Maven/Gradle compilation, PoV exploit replay, Semgrep static rules, and Lizard complexity metrics to analyze zero-shot patches without iterative tool-guided repair loops (Abstract, Sections 2, 3.1).
M2_Justification: Verifies all 319 patches across three automated dimensions—Axis 1 compilation, Axis 2 dynamic PoV exploit execution plus Semgrep static residual-flaw scanning, and Axis 3 full project unit test suites—aggregated into Security Repair Score (SRS) (Abstract, Section 3.1).
M3_Justification: Evaluates 319 patches (5 samples/bug) across 64 reproducible Java vulnerabilities spanning 21 CWEs in Vul4J, but tests only one LLM (Gemini 3.0 Flash) under a single zero-shot prompt (Abstract, Sections 4.1–4.2).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the replication package, failure taxonomy, and scoring scripts on GitHub (https://github.com/AmeerAlmaamari/LLM-Security-Patches-Analysis), though serving as an analytical study rather than a repair tool (Section 4).
Key_Strengths: Rigorous tri-axis validation (build + PoV + Semgrep + full unit tests) on 319 patches across 64 Vul4J CVEs; continuous Security Repair Score (SRS) and failure taxonomy; public GitHub repository.
Limitations: Evaluates only a single LLM (Gemini 3.0 Flash) and single zero-shot prompt on Java Vul4J; does not propose a tool-grounded repair pipeline.
Missing_Evidence: Multi-model and multi-language comparison; peer-reviewed venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: VulnResolver: A Hybrid Agent Framework for LLM-Based Automated Vulnerability Issue Resolution
M1_Justification: Combines ReAct exploration with structured repair via two sandboxed agents—CPCAgent (static analysis for repository dependency extraction) and SPAAgent (static analysis and dynamic execution to synthesize/verify violated safety properties)—followed by localization, patching, and selection (Abstract, Section 2.1).
M2_Justification: Verifies patches in isolated Docker containers via SEC-bench's automated secb build, PoC exploit sanitizer execution, and correctness oracles (Abstract, Sections 3.2, Threats to Validity).
M3_Justification: Benchmarked end-to-end (without oracle fault location or CWE labels) across 200 real-world C/C++ vulnerabilities from 29 repositories on SEC-bench Lite (75% resolution) and SEC-bench Full, outperforming OpenHands and SWE-agent with ablations (Abstract, Sections 3.1–3.2).
M4_Justification: Operates end-to-end from raw issue reports and PoCs without manual CWE/localization annotations inside Docker sandboxes, though omitting a public GitHub/Zenodo repository link in the text (Abstract, Sections 1, 3.2).
Key_Strengths: Eliminates manual fault-localization and CWE annotations via hybrid CPCAgent + SPAAgent safety-property synthesis; 75% resolution on SEC-bench Lite and SOTA on 200-CVE SEC-bench Full.
Limitations: Scoped to C/C++ SEC-bench repositories; no public replication repository URL provided in the manuscript.
Missing_Evidence: Public artifact/code release URL; cross-language evaluation; formal venue/DOI metadata.

Study_Title: PATCHEVAL: A New Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Patching Real-World Vulnerabilities
M1_Justification: Implements a containerized runtime sandbox harness supporting standalone LLMs and iterative feedback-guided agentic loops (SWE-Agent, OpenHands, commercial agent) with automated PoC and unit test execution (Abstract, Section 4.1).
M2_Justification: Verifies patches in isolated runtime sandboxes requiring both neutralization of reconstructed PoC exploits and passing of project unit test suites across 230 sandboxed CVEs (Abstract, Section 4, Table 3).
M3_Justification: Curates 1,000 real-world CVEs (2015–2025) across 65 CWEs in Go, JavaScript, and Python (230 full runtime sandboxes) and benchmarks 10 frontier/open LLMs plus 3 agents with token and dollar cost metrics (Abstract, Section 4.1, Table 3).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the PATCHEVAL dataset, Docker sandboxes, and evaluation harness on GitHub (https://github.com/bytedance/PatchEval) with granular token and API-cost benchmarks (Table 3, Conclusion).
Key_Strengths: Addresses multi-language gap with 1,000 CVEs (230 sandboxed) in Go, JavaScript, and Python; dual PoC + unit test validation; 10-LLM + 3-agent benchmark with cost metrics; public ByteDance GitHub release.
Limitations: Full runtime sandbox validation covers 230 of 1,000 CVEs due to manual PoC reconstruction effort; excludes C/C++/Rust.
Missing_Evidence: Formal peer-reviewed publication venue and DOI metadata.

Study_Title: VulnRepairEval: An Exploit-Based Evaluation Framework for Assessing Large Language Model Vulnerability Repair Capabilities
M1_Justification: Constructs a containerized differential exploit-testing harness to evaluate standalone LLMs and agentic scaffolds (SWE-Agent) in unified-diff generation, rather than proposing a tool-integrated repair architecture (Abstract, Sections 5.1, 6.1).
M2_Justification: Verifies patches via containerized differential execution requiring the real-world PoC exploit to succeed on the parent commit and fail on the patched code alongside build/functional checks (Abstract, Sections 5.2, 6.1).
M3_Justification: Evaluates 12 proprietary and open-source LLMs plus SWE-Agent, but across a small dataset of 23 Python CVEs constrained mainly to single-file contexts (Abstract, Sections 5.1, 6.1, 7).
M4_Justification: Commits to releasing evaluation scripts and pipeline code while withholding public PoCs for safety, demonstrating rigorous exploit validation though low current readiness (max 21.7% success) and no public GitHub link in text (Abstract, Sections 5, 7).
Key_Strengths: Stringent containerized differential PoC exploit validation across 12 frontier/open LLMs and SWE-Agent; highlights low real-world Python repair rates (<=21.7%).
Limitations: Small benchmark size (23 Python CVEs) mostly single-file; PoCs withheld; no public GitHub URL in text.
Missing_Evidence: Larger multi-language/multi-file evaluation corpus; public artifact link; peer-reviewed venue/DOI.

Study_Title: Eradicating the Unseen: Detecting, Exploiting, and Remediating a Path Traversal Vulnerability across GitHub
M1_Justification: Develops DotDotDefender, an automated pipeline combining static GitHub repository scanning, dynamic HTTP exploit confirmation of CWE-22 path traversal, CVSS scoring, GPT-4 patch synthesis, and automated post-patch verification before disclosure (Abstract, Sections 2, 3).
M2_Justification: Validates every GPT-4 patch dynamically in live Node.js execution by verifying server startup, benign HTTP GET behavior preservation, and blocking of path-traversal exploit payloads (Abstract, Section 3, Page 6).
M3_Justification: Scans GitHub at ecosystem scale (1,756 vulnerable open-source Node.js projects, 14% maintainer fix adoption after disclosure), though restricted to a single vulnerability pattern (CWE-22 Node.js file servers) and GPT-4 (Abstract, Sections 2.1, 9).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases DotDotDefender on GitHub (https://github.com/JafarAkhondali/DotDotDefender) and demonstrates live ecosystem deployment with responsible disclosures, two assigned CVEs, and 14% upstream maintainer patch adoption (Abstract, Footnote 4, Section 9).
Key_Strengths: Full end-to-end ecosystem pipeline (static scan -> dynamic exploit -> GPT-4 patch -> dynamic benign/exploit check -> responsible disclosure) across 1,756 GitHub projects; 2 CVEs assigned; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Scoped to a single CWE-22 Node.js static file-server pattern and a single LLM (GPT-4).
Missing_Evidence: Generalization across diverse CWE families and programming languages; official ACM AsiaCCS DOI.

Study_Title: VADER: A Human-Evaluated Benchmark for Vulnerability Assessment, Detection, Explanation, and Remediation
M1_Justification: Evaluates frontier LLMs in a standalone one-shot prompting setup across assessment, detection, explanation, and patch generation without static analyzers, compilers, sandboxes, or iterative tool loops (Abstract, Sections 3, 4).
M2_Justification: Assesses generated patches via double-annotated human security expert rubric grading (50% remediation quality, 20% explanation, 30% classification/test plan), without automated compilation, regression testing, or dynamic PoC replay (Abstract, Sections 3.1, 4).
M3_Justification: Curates 174 real-world multi-language vulnerabilities (Python, Java, JavaScript, C/C++, Go) and benchmarks six frontier LLMs (o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Grok 3 Beta, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.5) with confidence intervals and cross-task correlations (Abstract, Sections 3.1, 4).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases the VADER dataset, expert rubrics, and scoring tools on GitHub (https://github.com/AfterQuery/vader), though relying on manual expert rubric grading rather than automated CI/CD verification (Abstract, Section 6).
Key_Strengths: 174 expert double-annotated real-world multi-language vulnerabilities spanning assessment to remediation; benchmarks 6 frontier LLMs; public GitHub release.
Limitations: Relies on static human rubric grading rather than automated build, functional test, and dynamic exploit execution; one-shot prompting only without open-weight models.
Missing_Evidence: Automated execution-based functional and PoC exploit validation; peer-reviewed venue/DOI.

Study_Title: AutoPatch: Multi-Agent Framework for Patching Real-World CVEs Generated by Outdated LLMs
M1_Justification: Builds a multi-agent IDE/generation plugin combining semantic and data-flow analysis, unified CVE similarity retrieval over a post-cutoff vulnerability database, CoT vulnerability verification, and automated patch synthesis (Abstract, Sections I, III, Fig. 1).
M2_Justification: Validates detection/verification (F1 = 90.3%) and patch accuracy (94.1%) across 525 snippets from 75 high-severity CVEs using structured CoT verification criteria, without automated kernel/browser builds and dynamic PoC execution across targets (Abstract, Section V, Tables IV–V).
M3_Justification: Evaluates across 525 snippets from 75 post-cutoff high-severity CVEs (Linux kernel, Chrome, etc.) comparing reasoning models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) and baselines with >50x cost savings over fine-tuning, scoped to snippet-level evaluation on 75 CVEs (Abstract, Section V, Tables IV–V).
M4_Justification: Publicly releases AutoPatch on GitHub (https://github.com/ai-llm-research/autopatch), operates as a post-generation IDE security plugin for AI coding assistants, and cuts costs >50x vs. continual fine-tuning (Abstract, Sections I, IV).
